newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzanian inflation up,IMF says overall trend down.
newsitem.headline: Tanzanian inflation up,IMF says overall trend down.

text.p: Monthly inflation in Tanzania rose to 17.5 percent in March because of drought in the first quarter of the year but the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Friday the overall trend was down.

The Bank of Tanzania (BoT) in its monthly review said annual headline inflation as measured by change over 12 months in the consumer price indices increased from 13.8 percent in February to 17.5 percent in March.

"Similarly the seasonally adjusted food inflation increased from 17.7 percent in February to 28.5 percent in March due to increases in prices of staple foods following the prolonged drought in the country," the BoT's report said.
The BoT noted that food "carries more than 71 percent of the total weight in the composite consumer price index (CPI)".

"It may be noted that according to the Bureau of Statistics drought-adjusted inflation was only 13.5 percent for March 1997, reflecting the big impact of drought on the CPI during the month under review," the report said.
Festus Osunsade, IMF representative in Tanzania, said the IMF did not consider the March inflation figure as representing the underlying inflation trend in this country, which was down.

"When people went to buy food in March they paid more, true, but that is not the long-term trend. The normal trend is that inflation is coming down, and the drought is not a permanent feature in the economy, but an isolated problem," he said.

"The Tanzanian authorities are now working to revise the 17.5 figure because if you look apart from the food prices, from February to March the prices were stable and inflation in March actually came down to 13.5 percent.
"In normal circumstances inflation is continuing to go down -- there is nothing wrong in the way the government is managing the economy and the underlying trend is improving," he told Reuters.
In a related development Osunsade said a top executive from the IMF's Washington headquarters would visit Tanzania.
Alassane Ouattara, deputy managing director for the IMF, is due to arrive on May 17 for a four-day mission to discuss economic reforms by the government of President Benjamin Mkapa.
